title: Stack versus heap layout (where values and objects live)
hook: Every thread has a stack for local variables and call frames. The Common Language Runtime (CLR) garbage collector tracks objects on the managed heap. Struct versus class is about memory layout — not a promise that a struct never touches the heap.

blocks.text: The stack is per-thread storage for activation records: parameters, local variables, and return addresses. The managed heap is a region the CLR owns where reference-type objects and boxed values live. Value types store their data inline — on the stack when they are locals in a method frame, or inside a heap object when they are fields. Reference-type locals are pointers on the stack pointing at heap objects.

entries.plainDefinition: Per-thread memory for method frames. Fast push/pop; dies when the frame returns.
entries.example: An int local in a method lives in the current stack frame.

entries.plainDefinition: Memory region where the garbage collector allocates and tracks objects.
entries.example: new List<int>() allocates an object on the managed heap.

entries.plainDefinition: A type whose instances store data inline rather than as a separate heap object.
entries.example: int, bool, and record struct AuthStamp are value types.

entries.plainDefinition: A type whose instances are heap objects accessed through a reference.
entries.example: string and List<T> are reference types.

blocks.text: The garbage collector only walks the heap. Stack slots are roots: if a local still references a large byte buffer, that buffer stays alive. After the local goes out of scope, the next generation-0 collection can reclaim it. Boxing, closures, async state machines, and fields of heap objects are the usual reasons a struct ends up on the heap even though it is a value type.

blocks.title: Interview framing
blocks.body: Say: value types are inline; reference types are heap objects plus a reference. Locals can be on the stack until something promotes them — boxing, capture, or await.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Method call creates a frame
items.body: Parameters and value-type locals are laid out in the thread stack frame (or registers).

items.title: Reference types allocate on the heap
items.body: new creates a heap object; the local holds a managed reference to it.

items.title: Structs as fields live inside the object
items.body: A struct field of a class is stored inline in that object's heap layout.

items.title: Promotion events move data to the heap
items.body: Boxing, lambda capture, and async state machines can store value types on heap objects.

snippet.label: Same bytes, three homes
snippet.explanation: OnStack can stay in the frame. Boxed copies onto the heap as a boxed value. AcrossAwaitAsync stores stamp on the compiler-generated state machine object on the heap.

snippet.label: Reference local, heap object
snippet.explanation: The string object lives on the heap. The local token is a reference in the stack frame. ToCharArray allocates another heap array.

snippet.label: Struct field inside a class
snippet.explanation: The Session object is on the heap. AuthStamp is stored inline inside that object's layout — not as a separate allocation.

blocks.title: Primitives versus value types
rows: Structs and primitives can live in stack frames
No programmer-controlled stack struct for a record of two ints
Objects and closures always live in the V8 heap
Explicit or implicit boxing copies to heap
Numbers are not separate stack values like C# int
JS engine roots; you do not see stack frames

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Saying structs never go on the heap — boxing, async, and closures disprove that. Keeping a large byte[] in a long-lived singleton field for convenience. Ignoring that await extends the lifetime of locals onto the state machine object.

interviewTakeaways: Value types are inline; they are on the stack only when their container is a stack frame.
Async, lambdas, and boxing are the usual reasons a struct becomes a heap field.
Stack slots are garbage-collection roots for whatever they still reference.
commonPitfalls: Saying structs never go on the heap.
Keeping a large byte[] in a field of a long-lived singleton for convenience.
Ignoring that await extends the lifetime of locals to the state machine.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript numbers are not C# value types. Objects and closures always live in the JavaScript heap. There is no programmer-controlled stack struct for a record of two ints.
